newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cause of crash seen key to outlook on Brazil's TAM.
newsitem.headline: Cause of crash seen key to outlook on Brazil's TAM.

text.p: Brazilian airline TAM Lineas Aereas will suffer a short-term setback following Thursday's air tragedy, and analysts noted that the cause of the crash will be key to how soon its operations recover.

"If officials conclude that there was a failure in the aircraft's maintenance, this could have a serious impact on the company," Irineu Luiz Correa Filho, an analyst at Lopes Filho consulting firm, said.
Brazilian aviation officials said they had recovered the ill-fated airplane's two black boxes and said a final report would be published within 90 days.
TAM, an aggressive regional carrier, had seen its number of passengers rise almost 200 percent to 4.5 million over the course of three years.
Analysts agree that its number of passengers is likely to fall in the near-term. How fast the airline's image and operations recover will depend on TAM's strategy in addressing the crash, they added.
All 96 passengers on board and at least eight persons on the ground were killed as a Rio-bound Fokker-100 ploughed into a Sao Paulo neighborhood shortly after take-off Thursday morning.
"The psychological impact of the crash is likely to reduce the number of passengers in the short-term," said Correa Filho.
Analysts also raised questions on how much TAM will have to spend to compensate the families of those killed in the accident.

A TAM spokeswoman said the firm had no immediate estimate on compensation. But lawyer Luiz Antonio de Oliveira Mello, head of an aviation consumer's group, predicted TAM may spend some $30 million on compensations.
Until Thursday's disaster, TAM shares had been highly recommended by most analysts, who saw the company as the cream of the aviation sector due to its hot growth prospects.
TAM developed a niche transporting businessmen to and from Brazil's prosperous but small towns in the country's vast interior.
The company uses a fleet of Fokker-100 aircraft, which require only low maintenance, and have contributed to the firm's high profitability, analysts said.
Last Tuesday, TAM announced plans to launch non-stop routes between Brazil and the United States, and between major Brazilian state capitals.
The announcement followed TAM's recent acquisition of Paraguay's Lapsa airline in a bid to expand its presence in the Mercosur trade bloc.
TAM, which has consistently shown earnings gains, reported a $23.3 million net profit for the first half of 1996.
Net profits for 1995 were $43.9 million against $18.1 million the previous year.
The company had estimated 1996 revenues of $600 million, against $454 million last year.
The firm's preferred stock, which had risen 137.6 percent in dollar terms so far this year, plunged 22.3 percent on the Sao Paulo bourse on Thursday following news of the crash.
Today the stock recouped some of those losses, rising 6.1 percent to 53.60 reais.
-- Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 232 4411
